title: Latency hunt: edge routing & cache jitter journal
content:
Purpose / short story:
- Quick personal journal for an ongoing latency investigation across edge routing + prefix cache warmers. Not a formal runbook; capture commands, one-offs, and next small experiments so I don't forget between shifts.

Top-level hypothesis: sporadic ~200-400ms p99 spikes are correlated with cache-miss bursts + a single egress path flapping in ams region. Could be batching fallback + cold KV fetch + slow route.

Observations so far (timestamps local):
- 2024-10-16 09:40: observed p99 jump from ~85ms -> 320ms for ~7 minutes on route /v1/generate in ams-edge pool. No pod restarts.
- 2024-10-16 09:41 logs: many requests falling back from cached prefix (cache hit rate dropped from 94% -> 24%).
- 2024-10-16 09:43 netstat on edge-gw-2 shows transient retransmits on eth0 -> possible path degradation to backend.
- 2024-10-17 14:20 repeat spike correlated with a deploy to dedicated-gw (canary) in same AZ. Timing suspicious.

Quick checklist to run when spike happens (short commands + notes):
- 1) Confirm metric windows:
  - grafana: time range quick = last 15m, panel = /v1/generate p99 latency by route and model.
  - query: sum(rate(requests_total[1m])) by (route, pool) and cache_hit_rate over same range.
- 2) Check edge cache stats (redis-ish)
  - redis-cli -h edge-cache-ams-01 INFO stats | egrep "hits|misses|expired"
  - if miss rate > 30%: run prefix dump: curl -s http://edge-cache-ams-01:7000/prefixes | jq '. | length'
- 3) Quick host networking:
  - ssh edge-gw-2: sudo ip -s link show eth0; sudo tc -s qdisc show dev eth0
  - check dmesg for NIC errors: sudo dmesg | tail -n 120 | egrep -i "error|link|rx|tx"
- 4) If single host shows issues, temporarily drain: kubectl drain node/edge-gw-2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60 (note: inform SRE rota first)

Experiments to isolate root cause:
- A) Canary bypass cache path: add header X-Force-Cache: true/false in a small load test to compare latency with cache hits suppressed. Workload: apachebench -c 40 -n 400 against ams-edge with header toggles.
- B) Controlled warmup: run synthetic prefix warmers with varying QPS (5->50) to map where cache hit rate collapses. Script: scripts/warmup-prefixes.sh --region ams --qps 20 --duration 300
- C) Route-level packet capture: tcpdump -i eth0 port 443 and filter to backend IP for 30s around spike; upload pcap to /tmp/pcaps for analysis (note: pcap sensitive, remove after).

Things I suspect but haven't validated:
- - Cache eviction policy overloaded by a tiny set of long-tail prefixes; warmers thrash resident set when cold traffic arrives.
- - Single egress NAT gateway in ams experiencing burst congestion -> increases backend RTT -> runtime falls back to blocking batching -> amplifies latency.
- - A recent kernel update on a small subset of nodes (ams-edge-*) changed TCP pacing defaults (see ticket KERNEL-2024-09).

Notes to self: safe mitigations to try in urgent incident
- Immediately increase cache size quota on ams-edge cache nodes (if disk / mem available) and restart warmers with longer TTL.
- Temporarily move traffic to ams-edge-2 pool (set routing policy weight +1) to evict weird host.
- Apply circuit-breaker short window to batcher: max_queue_ms=30 to reduce tail amplification (but check throughput impact).

Small experiments I want to run this week (owner / ETA):
- Meera: run warmup-sweep across all ams-edge shards, capture hit-rate curves (ETA: 2024-10-23).
- Samir: verify NAT gateway metrics and egress errors (ETA: 2024-10-22).
- Riley (me): add tracepoint in runtime to log cache eviction events with small sample rate 1/1000 (ETA: 2024-10-25).

Snippets / commands I've used (paste for later):
- curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -H 'X-Force-Cache: false' https://ams-edge.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"x"}' | jq '.latency'
- kubectl get pods -n infra -l app=edge-cache -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=edge-gw-2
- sudo perf top -p $(pgrep edge-runtime) --call-graph dwarf (for live CPU hot spots)

Unresolved questions / TODOs (short):
- Is there a single NAT egress for the AZ or per-node SNAT? (pinged networking)
- Can we get a pcap from the time window with TLS fingerprints to see if repeated TLS handshakes are contributing? (security approval needed)
- Is the cache TTL policy aligned with QPS spikes from downstream customers (not all routes have same prefix churn)?

When I'm done with this doc:
- Move validated steps to a formal runbook under confluence: confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Edge+Latency+Runbook (placeholder).
- Clean up pcaps + any temporary keys.

Misc brain-dumps (notes to self):
- Consider eBPF-based per-socket latency histogram to avoid pcap for next time.
- If batching fallback is the main amplifier, a tiny windowed-smoothing (exponential) on batch size decision could reduce p99 at cost of a few avg ms.

End of scratch. Keep short and actionable. Revisit after Meera and Samir results.
